issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness. Ambulances and pregnancy/birth reminders could fit certain illness contexts, but physical affection as a trigger is hard to reconcile without any supporting illness-related memory or appraisal content, and the three triggers together do not suggest a single coherent illness narrative.

Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/ambient danger vigilance (needing back to wall, reacting to sudden movements, constant environmental scanning), which reads more like fear of assault or attack than threat linked to life-threatening illness. With the given trauma type, this pattern is hard to explain unless supported by corresponding trauma content, which is absent.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport does not match the rest of the profile. No trigger, threat, or memory item suggests transport-related trauma cues or a reason this strategy would be central for this illness-based PTSD presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Rage on recall is not impossible, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the memory content and the illness trauma type. The memories are otherwise characterized by somatic/nonverbal reliving, while the threat pattern is hypervigilance to external attack; intense rage does not help unify these elements into one coherent formulation.

For a trauma type of life-threatening illness, ambulances and hospital smells are plausible triggers, but pregnancy/childbirth reminders are hard to reconcile unless the illness was specifically pregnancy-related; as presented, this trigger set does not describe a coherent illness-linked cue pattern.

issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport appears disconnected from the rest of the profile: no trigger or threat item involves buses/trains/crowds, and no formulation edge suggests triggers are driving this strategy. It looks like a strategy aimed at a symptom context not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by hypervigilance to interpersonal/physical attack cues (needing back to wall, reacting to others' sudden movements, scanning the room), which fits assault/combat-type danger more than illness-related trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: These threat items do not connect plausibly to the listed illness-related triggers (hospital smell, needles/medical equipment); the cross-node pattern mixes medical trauma cues with a separate attack-style threat state.

issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall is possible, but here it sits oddly with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear-based medical reminders and attack-style vigilance rather than anger-related meanings or appraisals.

issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is hard to link coherently to the rest of this illness-related profile, which otherwise centers on hospital/medical cues; this strategy appears to address a different trigger context not represented elsewhere.

issues.explanation: Hypervigilance to sudden movements by others is a poor fit with the selected medical/illness triggers and memories, which suggest hospital procedures and bodily trauma rather than interpersonal attack or assault-type threat.

issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall is not well supported by the other selected items or the trauma type; the surrounding profile reflects fear, bodily re-experiencing, and medical triggers rather than anger-focused meaning or appraisals.

vignette:
Anna Müller is a 41-year-old firefighter who had spent most of her career moving toward emergencies rather than away from them. What unsettled her was not a fireground injury or a call gone wrong, but the months when she became critically ill with a life-threatening infection that required repeated hospital admissions, IV lines, and invasive examinations. She remembers flashes of white light, the sharp medicinal sting of antiseptic on her skin, the sight of needles and dripping bags above her bed. What comes back most strongly is bodily: her shoulders pinning into the mattress, one arm held still for a line, her whole body braced in dread while staff worked over her. When she tries to explain that period now, she falters. She says she knows what happened, but cannot seem to put the worst of it into words; instead the memory arrives as terror and posture, as if her body has gone back there before her mind can speak.

After she recovered enough to return home, reminders of medical settings began to hit her with a force she did not expect. Passing through the ER entrance at work, catching the smell of antiseptic on a medic’s gloves, or seeing IV equipment and needles during a call could make her body jolt into alarm. During her own follow-up appointments, the exam room was often the worst of all. Her heart would pound, her muscles would lock, and she would begin scanning the room automatically—for the tray, the tubing, the clinician’s hands, the door—like someone preparing for an immediate threat. The reminders did not feel symbolic to Anna; they felt dangerous in themselves, as though her body had learned that these sights and smells meant she was again helpless and at risk.

The memory also continued to live close to the surface in a more private way. When it came back, it brought the same terror she had felt in the hospital, and with it the sense of being physically arranged exactly as she had been during those procedures. Because the recall was so overwhelming and so hard to describe, Anna began cutting it off wherever she could. If an image or body-sensation rose up, she would force herself to think about something else—equipment checks, station chores, dinner plans, anything with edges and order. She also started avoiding situations that might stir up strong feelings more broadly, because once she felt herself getting emotionally activated, she feared the hospital sensations would break through.

Over the following months those habits spread into her daily life. At the firehouse, where ambulances pull in and out and medical gear is part of the ordinary environment, Anna quietly rearranged tasks so she was less often near the medic bay. She lingered in the apparatus area if crews were restocking supplies, and she found reasons not to look directly at IV kits or procedure trays. She postponed her own physical examinations and dreaded any suggestion of tests. In the moment, redirecting her mind and steering clear of medical cues gave her a brief sense of control. But because she was always shutting the experience down rather than letting it take shape in words, the memory stayed raw, more like an assault on her body than something that had happened in the past.

That rawness kept her on guard. The less room she gave herself to feel or think about what had happened, the more persistently tense she became. Even on ordinary shifts she noticed herself constantly scanning for danger, not only on calls but in hallways, supply rooms, and break areas where a passing antiseptic smell or glimpse of a needle could appear without warning. Her body seemed perpetually ready to react. And because she was watching so hard for signs that something medical might confront her, those cues stood out everywhere. A disinfectant wipe on a counter, a coworker mentioning a hospital transfer, a routine occupational health reminder could seize her attention immediately and trigger another surge of physical alarm.

By the time Anna sought help, her world had narrowed in ways that embarrassed her. She was still showing up for work, but doing so with mounting strain, quietly structuring her day around what to avoid. At home, her husband had begun to notice that she became distant whenever medical issues came up, changing the subject abruptly rather than risk the feelings underneath. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was starting to fear not just hospitals, but her own reactions to anything that reminded her of them. She wants, more than anything, to be able to walk into an exam room or handle medical equipment at work without her body acting as if she is back on that bed, trapped and terrified.
